issues.legal_issue: A claimant obtains statutory occupancy status from a revenue entry only when the qualifying record shows the claimant as an occupant and the entry is not fraudulent.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a revenue record from the relevant year, but the claimant's name appeared in the remarks column rather than as an occupant in the cultivator column.
The claimant was not recorded in the prescribed manner as an occupant, and the record contained evidence that the entry had been made surreptitiously.
A consolidated record showed the land cultivated by its owners and did not record the claimant as a sub-tenant.
issues.conclusion: The entry did not qualify the claimant for adhivasi rights under section 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, the qualifying revenue entry, rather than proof of actual possession, is ordinarily decisive; cases of fraud are excepted. Amba Prasad v. Abdul Noor Khan, [1964] 7 S.C.R. 800, explains that the provision accepts the relevant record and eliminates inquiry into disputed actual possession. The entry must record the claimant as an occupant, not merely mention the claimant in another column.

predicates.occupancy_status_claim_based_on_revenue_: A person claims statutory occupancy status on the basis of a revenue record for the relevant period.
predicates.entry_does_not_record_occupant_status: The relevant record does not identify the claimant as an occupant in the manner required for that status.
predicates.entry_is_fraudulent: The relevant entry was made fraudulently or surreptitiously.

issues.definition: When a person relies on a revenue record for occupancy status, a record that does not show occupant status or is fraudulent does not confer that status.

issues.legal_issue: A person must have lawful cultivatory possession to qualify for statutory rights based on possession during the specified agricultural year, and forcible or surreptitious occupation without a right does not qualify.
material_facts: The claimant had no established right to occupy the land and was not shown to have possessed it through the end of the preceding agricultural year.
The records did not establish actual cultivatory possession during the relevant year, and the claimant offered no direct evidence of such possession.
The claimant was recorded as a sub-tenant without settlement of rent, but did not claim or prove a tenancy agreement with the owners.
The owners denied that they had leased the land to the claimant or received rent from the claimant.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not establish cultivatory possession qualifying for adhivasi rights under section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952; wrongful occupation could not confer those rights against the owners.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952, requires a claimant to establish cultivatory possession during the specified year and grants rights against tenure holders to persons who had been admitted to such possession. The Explanation excludes specified forms of participation in cultivation. The Court held that qualifying cultivatory possession must be lawful and for the whole year; a trespasser who forcibly or surreptitiously occupies land does not qualify. Ram Krishna v. Bhagwan Baksh Singh, [1961] A.L.J. 301, was approved, and Nanhoo Mal v. Muloo, I.L.R. [1963] All. 751, was disapproved.

predicates.claim_under_possession_based_land_rights: A claimant seeks statutory land rights based on cultivatory possession during a specified period.
predicates.actual_cultivatory_possession_establishe: Evidence establishes that the claimant actually cultivated the land throughout the required period.
predicates.forcible_occupation_without_right: The claimant entered or remained on the land by force or surreptitiously without a lawful right to occupy it.

issues.definition: A claim to land rights based on cultivatory possession fails when actual possession for the required period is not established or the occupation was forcible and without right.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court's factual findings are not binding in a second appeal when the court ignored material evidence or misread the record.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the claimant was recorded as an occupant and was in cultivatory possession.

It did not address important evidence bearing on whether the revenue entries were genuine, including conflicting certified extracts and a consolidated record that did not show the claimant in possession.
Its conclusion on cultivatory possession relied partly on a misreading of the earlier revenue entry and on inferences unsupported by the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not bound by the first appellate court's findings and could reject them in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A finding of fact is not binding in a second appeal where the first appellate court ignored important evidence or misread the record. The Court applied that principle to the findings concerning both the revenue entries and cultivatory possession; no statutory provision or earlier case was identified for this point.

predicates.second_appeal_from_first_appellate_findi: A second appeal challenges factual findings made by a first appellate court.
predicates.first_appellate_court_ignored_material_e: The first appellate court failed to consider important evidence or materially misread the record.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, factual findings need not be followed when the first appellate court ignored material evidence or misread the record.

issues.legal_issue: A court may allow amendment of a plaint and grant possession in a suit that was competent when filed when a defendant obtains possession from another court during the litigation.
material_facts: The land had been attached in proceedings under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the parties were directed to establish their rights in a civil suit.
The plaintiffs initially sought a declaration of their rights and an injunction while the land remained under attachment.
During the litigation, the defendant obtained possession from the criminal court pursuant to the first appellate court's decision.
After the plaintiffs succeeded on the merits, the High Court allowed them to amend the plaint to seek possession.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified and bound to allow the amendment and grant possession, and the defendant could not use an order obtained during the litigation to displace the civil court's jurisdiction over a suit that was competent when filed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was relevant to the attachment and the direction to litigate rights in a competent civil court. The Court held that, where the suit was competent when filed and possession was obtained from another court during its pendency, the court could allow amendment and make an order consistent with the rights it declared, avoiding renewed litigation. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: civil_suit_competent_when_filed and land_attached_in_criminal_proceeding and defendant_obtained_possession_during_suit_from_another_court and plaintiffs_succeed_on_rights

predicates.civil_suit_competent_when_filed: The plaintiffs filed a civil suit that was within the civil court's competence when commenced.
predicates.land_attached_in_criminal_proceeding: The land was attached in a criminal proceeding in which the parties were directed to establish their rights in a civil court.
predicates.defendant_obtained_possession_during_sui: During the civil suit, the defendant obtained possession from another court or its officer.
predicates.plaintiffs_succeed_on_rights: The court decides the plaintiffs' underlying rights in their favour.

issues.definition: When a competent civil suit concerns attached land, the defendant obtains possession from another court during the suit, and the plaintiffs prevail on their rights, the court may allow a possession amendment and decree possession.
